questions.q: How does the force from the brake pedal reach the wheels in a hydraulic braking system?
options: Through a taut metal cable
Through compressed air alone, in every private car
Through a rubber belt from the engine
Through pressure that travels in brake fluid, in pipes
questions.explain: In a hydraulic system, pressure on the pedal becomes pressure in the brake fluid, which travels through pipes to every wheel.

questions.q: What does the brake servo (booster) do?
options: Drain air from the system
Split pressure between front and rear
Prevent wheel lock
Boost the force of your foot on the pedal, so braking takes less effort
questions.explain: The brake servo, using vacuum or pressure, boosts the force of your foot on the pedal so braking needs less effort.

questions.q: Why is the braking system split into two separate hydraulic circuits?
options: To save on brake fluid
It’s a requirement only for electric cars
So that even if one circuit leaks, some braking stays active
To increase the car’s speed
questions.explain: Splitting into two separate circuits (for example diagonally) ensures a leak in one circuit doesn’t cancel all braking ability.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of a disc brake over a drum brake?
options: It doesn’t need pads at all
It cools faster and keeps stopping consistent with repeated use
It’s cheaper to manufacture
It’s heavier, so it’s more stable
questions.explain: The brake disc is exposed to air and cools quickly, so it keeps performing consistently even with repeated braking, unlike the enclosed drum.

questions.q: What does a thin, steady squeal when braking mean?
options: Low tyre pressure
A fault in the torque converter
A metal wear tab warning that the pad is close to its minimum
A problem with the clutch
questions.explain: Most cars have a metal tab that touches the disc when the pad is nearly worn out, producing a warning squeal.

questions.q: The brake pedal sinks deep and feels “soft”. What does this suggest?
options: Tyre pressure too high
Air in the pipes or a brake fluid leak
Pads that are too new
The gearbox has shifted into too high a gear
questions.explain: A soft pedal that sinks deep usually points to air in the pipes or a fluid leak — the system needs bleeding.

questions.q: The car pulls sharply to one side on every stop. What’s the likely cause?
options: Tyre pressure too high in all the tyres
A pad that’s too new on that side
Neutral gear while braking
A caliper stuck on that side, or oil/water on one pad
questions.explain: Pulling to one side when braking usually points to a caliper stuck on that side, or contamination on one pad.

questions.q: You hear a deep metal grinding sound on every stop. What’s the right thing to do?
options: Drive straight to a garage with maximum care, without pressing hard on the brakes
Add engine oil to the brakes
Keep driving normally until your next garage appointment
Ignore it — it’s normal in a new car
questions.explain: Deep metal grinding means the pad is completely worn out and metal is damaging the disc — don’t wait with this.

questions.q: What does ABS do in an emergency stop?
options: Drains air from the braking system
Always halves the stopping distance
Releases and reapplies the brake at the same wheel repeatedly, to prevent lock-up and preserve steering
Changes gear on its own
questions.explain: ABS stops the wheels from locking under hard braking, so the driver can keep steering and swerve around an obstacle.

questions.q: What does electronic brakeforce distribution (EBD) do?
options: Warm up the brakes before driving
Lock the driveshaft when parked
Adjust the split of braking force between the front and rear wheels in real time, according to load
Increase the car’s speed
questions.explain: EBD splits braking strength between front and rear according to the car’s load, to maximise stability and stopping power.

questions.q: How do you brake correctly in an emergency stop in a car with ABS?
options: Press hard and keep pressing, even if you feel a pulsing in the pedal
Shift to neutral and then brake
Press gently so as not to trigger the ABS
Press and release alternately, like manual “pumping”
questions.explain: In a car with ABS you press hard without easing off; the pulsing in the pedal is a sign the system is working normally.

questions.q: What does the brake assist system detect?
options: A tyre with low pressure
D mode in an automatic gearbox
A pad that’s completely worn out
A fast, panicked emergency stamp on the pedal, and it automatically adds maximum braking pressure
questions.explain: Brake assist detects the fast pedal push typical of a genuine panic, and adds maximum braking pressure automatically.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the parking brake and the regular hydraulic braking system?
options: The parking brake only works when the ABS is faulty
There’s no difference, it’s exactly the same system
The parking brake works only with air pressure
The parking brake works entirely separately, usually mechanically and only on the rear wheels
questions.explain: The parking brake is independent of the hydraulic system — it usually engages only the rear brakes, mechanically, by cable.

questions.q: When should you apply the parking brake?
options: Only on an especially steep slope
Only in a car with a manual gearbox
Every time you park, even in an automatic car in P
Only when the engine is off for more than an hour
questions.explain: Apply the parking brake every time you park, even in an automatic car in P — it doesn’t depend on the hydraulic brakes.

questions.q: What is true about hill-hold assist?
options: It prevents rolling backward for only a few seconds, between lifting off the brake and pressing the accelerator
It only works in a car with a manual gearbox
It’s a full substitute for the parking brake, even for extended parking
It applies the brakes permanently until the engine is switched off
questions.explain: Hill-hold assist is temporary only — it helps during the switch from the brake to the accelerator on a slope, and isn’t a substitute for the parking brake when actually parked.

questions.q: What happens if you drive with the parking brake partly engaged without noticing?
options: The rear brakes heat up and wear out fast
The car becomes more fuel-efficient
It has no effect at all
The car’s speed increases
questions.explain: A parking brake that’s partly engaged while driving heats up the rear brakes and wears them out fast.

questions.q: What is brake fade?
options: A temporary drop in braking effectiveness caused by overheating, mainly on a long descent
An automatic shift into a low gear
A fault in the torque converter
A light that warns of low air pressure
questions.explain: Brake fade is a temporary drop in braking effectiveness caused by the pads and discs overheating.

questions.q: What’s the right way to slow down on a long, steep descent, to prevent brake fade?
options: Drive in a high gear and brake hard at the last moment
Shift to neutral and avoid using the brakes entirely
Use engine braking with a low gear, and brake only with short, firm stops
Press gently and continuously on the brake for the whole descent
questions.explain: Engine braking in a low gear keeps you at a safe speed with almost no need to touch the brake; a light, continuous push actually heats the brakes the most.

questions.q: What happens when the brake fluid boils from extreme heat?
options: Tyre pressure rises
Air bubbles form in the pipes, and the pedal sinks deep and feels soft
The engine switches off automatically
The brakes become stronger
questions.explain: Boiling brake fluid creates compressible air bubbles in the pipes; you’re pressing on air instead of fluid, and the pedal turns soft and sinks deep — brake failure.

questions.q: Why do heavy vehicles need air brakes rather than hydraulic brakes?
options: Because the law bans brake fluid in heavy vehicles
Because it allows far greater braking force, needed for the heavy vehicle’s weight
Because it’s easier to maintain than a hydraulic brake
Because air is cheaper than brake fluid
questions.explain: Air brakes provide far greater braking force than a regular hydraulic brake — essential for a heavy vehicle’s weight.

questions.q: The air pressure warning light and buzzer are on before you set off. What do you do?
options: Set off and wait for the pressure to rise while driving
Turn off the buzzer and drive carefully
Add air at a petrol station before continuing
Don’t move until the pressure reaches the normal range
questions.explain: You must not move when air pressure is below the normal range — the buzzer and light are warning exactly of this, and it’s a risk of losing your brakes.

questions.q: Why is the spring brake considered a “fail-safe” design?
options: Because if air pressure suddenly drops, the spring locks the brakes on its own, without the driver doing anything
Because it renews itself automatically without maintenance
Because it doesn’t depend on air pressure at all
Because it’s meant only for parking on a gentle slope
questions.explain: A strong spring pushes the spring brake into the locked position, and it’s air pressure that releases it; a sudden pressure drop makes it lock on its own — the fault stops the vehicle.

questions.q: Why do you drain water from a heavy vehicle’s air tanks as part of the daily check?
options: Because moisture that collects as water can freeze in winter and rust the tank
Because the law only requires this once a year
To increase the vehicle’s speed
To reduce the vehicle’s weight
questions.explain: The air entering the system carries moisture that collects as water at the bottom of the tank; daily draining prevents freezing in winter and rust.

questions.q: What does a retarder do on a heavy vehicle?
options: Slow the vehicle on long descents without wearing the brake pads
Raise the air pressure in the tanks
Lock the spring brake
Change gear automatically on an incline
questions.explain: The retarder is an additional braking system, usually hydraulic or electric, that slows the vehicle on long descents without wearing the friction brakes.
